content:
Christian apologists often rest the case on one verse: "apart from shedding of blood there is no remission" (Hebrews 9:22). On this argument God forgives no sin until blood is shed, and the death of Jesus (peace be upon him) is the one way to forgiveness, which Islam has refused.[1]

The verse is real, and blood has a real place in the sacrifices of the Torah. The question is whether the Bible teaches that God is unable to forgive without it.

This article aims to provide context to that claim, insha'Allah, through five passages from the Torah, the Psalms, the prophets and Hebrews itself. The Quran states its own principle at the outset: "It is not their meat nor their blood, that reaches Allah: it is your piety that reaches Him" (22:37).[2]

"For the life of the flesh is in the blood; and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life" (Leviticus 17:11).[3]

The verse comes in a chapter that regulates slaughter and forbids eating blood. It ties blood to life and gives it a role at the altar.

Christian readers take the verse as a figure of the death of Jesus, and Hebrews makes the comparison at length. We grant the verse its plain weight: in Israel's worship, blood makes atonement. The verse states no rule that God can forgive in no other way, and the same book of Leviticus shows another way.

Leviticus 5 sets out the sin offering on a sliding scale. A person who cannot afford a lamb brings two birds, and one who cannot afford the birds brings "one tenth of an ephah of fine flour for a sin offering" (5:11).[4]

Then verse 13: "The priest shall make atonement for him concerning his sin that he has sinned in any of these things, and he will be forgiven."[4] No blood is shed in that offering, and the Torah calls the man forgiven.

A Christian can reply that the flour still belongs to a system of sacrifice built on blood. That is true, and it grants our point: inside the Torah's own law, a poor man's sin was forgiven with no death at all.

The verse is usually quoted from its second half. Its first half reads: "According to the law, nearly everything is cleansed with blood" (Hebrews 9:22).[5] The author is speaking of the sanctuary, the covenant and its rites of cleansing, and he qualifies his own statement.

The New American Bible, the translation of the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, says so in its note on the verse. "Ancient Israel did envisage other means of obtaining forgiveness", it states, naming contrition, fasting and almsgiving, and "the author is limiting his horizon to the sacrificial cult".[6]

Hebrews argues that the death of Jesus achieves what the old sacrifices could not, since "it is impossible that the blood of bulls and goats should take away sins" (10:4).[5] It makes that argument about the cult, and the Catholic bishops' own edition declines to stretch it into a rule for all forgiveness.

Psalm 51 is the Bible's great prayer of repentance. It opens: "Have mercy on me, God, according to your loving kindness. According to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions" (51:1).[7]

Then: "For you don't delight in sacrifice, or else I would give it. You have no pleasure in burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. A broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (51:16 to 17).[7]

The psalm closes by speaking well of sacrifices rightly offered, so it keeps Israel's worship in place. It sets an order within that worship, and the turning of the heart comes first. Hosea puts it in one line, "For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice" (6:6), and Jesus quotes the line twice in Matthew (9:13; 12:7).[8]

Ezekiel 18 is a chapter-long argument about personal responsibility: "But if the wicked turns from all his sins that he has committed, and keeps all my statutes, and does that which is lawful and right, he shall surely live. He shall not die. None of his transgressions that he has committed will be remembered against him" (18:21 to 22).[9] The chapter names no sacrifice.

Jonah gives the same principle as a story. Nineveh fasts and turns from violence, and "God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way. God relented of the disaster which he said he would do to them" (Jonah 3:10).[10] The city is spared, and no offering is recorded.

Christian theology answers that such forgiveness rested in advance on the cross, though no one in Nineveh knew of it. That is a reading of the whole canon from its end. The texts themselves show God forgiving the repentant, and name no innocent life taken first.

The churches explain the death of Jesus in more than one way. The Catechism of the Catholic Church calls it "the Paschal sacrifice that accomplishes the definitive redemption of men", a sacrifice that "completes and surpasses all other sacrifices", by which "Jesus atoned for our faults and made satisfaction for our sins to the Father".[11] The Orthodox Church in America describes redemption above all as "the destruction of death by Christ's own death", and calls the language of payment and ransom metaphorical.[12]

The Quran answers from its own premise. God forgives the one who turns to Him and asks for no blood: "O my Servants who have transgressed against their souls! Despair not of the Mercy of Allah: for Allah forgives all sins", and then, "Turn ye to our Lord (in repentance)" (39:53 to 54).[13]

Repentance (tawbah), as al-Nawawi sets out its conditions, means leaving the sin, regretting it and resolving never to return to it, and, where another person was wronged, restoring that person's right.[14] Each sinner carries his own repentance. Al-Fārūqī reads the Quran's account of man the same way: he begins "ethically sane and sound, not weighed down by any original sin", and he needs no saviour.[15]

The bottom line

Blood has a real place in Leviticus, and Hebrews gives the death of Jesus a decisive sacrificial meaning. The rule that God can forgive nothing without blood goes further than the Bible goes. Leviticus forgives the poor man who brings flour, Psalm 51 sets the contrite heart first, Ezekiel promises life to the wicked man who turns, Nineveh is spared, and the Catholic bishops' note limits Hebrews 9:22 to the cult.

Christian theology joins those passages through the cross. The Quran reads them as they stand: God forgives the one who repents, and "no bearer of burdens can bear the burden of another" (6:164).[2] We set out the Quran's account of the end of Jesus in our article on the crucifixion and Quran 4:157. Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Hebrews 9:22 (World English Bible). For the argument, see Christian Research Institute, "Is the Shedding of Blood Necessary for Forgiveness?", equip.org, which holds that in the New Testament forgiveness requires the sacrifice of a substitute.
  2. Quran 22:37; 6:164, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  3. Leviticus 17:10 to 14 (World English Bible).
  4. Leviticus 5:7 to 13 (World English Bible).
  5. Hebrews 9:11 to 28; 10:4 (World English Bible).
  6. New American Bible, Revised Edition, note on Hebrews 9:22, on the website of the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, bible.usccb.org.
  7. Psalm 51:1, 16 to 19 (World English Bible).
  8. Hosea 6:6; Matthew 9:13; 12:7 (World English Bible).
  9. Ezekiel 18:1 to 32 (World English Bible).
  10. Jonah 3:5 to 10 (World English Bible).
  11. Catechism of the Catholic Church, 613 to 615.
  12. Orthodox Church in America, "Redemption", in The Orthodox Faith, vol. 1, Doctrine and Scripture, "The Symbol of Faith".
  13. Quran 39:53 to 54, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  14. Al-Nawawī, Riyāḍ al-Ṣāliḥīn, chapter 2, "On Repentance", introduction.
  15. Ismāʿīl Rājī al-Fārūqī, Al Tawhid: Its Implications for Thought and Life, 2nd ed. (Herndon, VA: International Institute of Islamic Thought, 1992), chapter 1.
